claims.text: At fixed valence electron count, mixing-entropy-driven compositional disorder primarily governs superconducting transition temperature in high-entropy alloys.
At fixed valence electron count, mixing-entropy-driven compositional disorder primarily governs superconducting transition sharpness in high-entropy alloys.
Higher mixing entropy increases random local potential fluctuations.
Local potential fluctuations diminish effective electron-phonon coupling.
Mixing-entropy-driven disorder reduces the density of states at the Fermi level.
Increased mixing entropy suppresses Tc.
Increased mixing entropy broadens the superconducting transition.
(TaNb)1-x(ZrHfTi)x is a superconducting bcc high-entropy-alloy system.
The proposed initial (TaNb)1-x(ZrHfTi)x sample is equiatomic and well characterized.
A binary or ternary comparator can be engineered to match the valence electron count of the equiatomic five-component alloy while differing primarily in mixing entropy.
The degree of atomic-scale chemical disorder can be quantified through lattice strain, XRD peak broadening, or scanning tunneling microscopy.
Atomic-scale compositional disorder affects electron scattering.
Atomic-scale compositional disorder modulates the phonon spectrum.
The superconducting (TaNb)1-x(ZrHfTi)x system is consistent with BCS superconductivity in the dirty limit.
Stronger disorder-induced electron scattering lowers Tc within the dirty-limit BCS framework.
The high-mixing-entropy alloy should have lower Tc and a broader heat-capacity transition than the electron-count-matched low-entropy alloy.
Mean free path should remain roughly comparable between the high- and low-mixing-entropy comparison alloys.
A critical amount of disorder can suppress superconductivity near an Anderson quantum phase transition.
Significant changes in electron count can alter Tc through density-of-states changes rather than through disorder.
Subtle microstructural differences could confound any isolated effect of mixing entropy on Tc and transition width.

contradictions.description: The mechanism predicts that higher mixing entropy causes stronger electron scattering, but the predicted outcome says that mean free path, an electron-scattering indicator, should remain roughly comparable between the high- and low-entropy alloys.
